Sallowpoint in November smelled of wet slate, woodsmoke, and the long, sour mudflats exposed by the morning tide. Arthur Vance walked up from the railway halt with his leather tool roll tucked beneath his arm like a rolled umbrella, keeping close to the granite shopfronts to stay out of the crosswind. Most of the shutters along Hill Street were drawn for the season. The chandler’s window displayed coils of tarred hemp and a brass barometer set permanently to *Change*; next door, the bakery had closed sometime in the nineties, leaving only a faded gold-leaf crescent above the lintel.

He was fifty-eight, a man whose hands had grown thick at the knuckles from forty years of coaxing stubborn metal, though his fingertips remained strangely sensitive, the skin smoothed by watchmaker’s oil and polishing rouge. He no longer repaired wristwatches—his eyes resented the strain of hairsprings no wider than a human eyelash—and instead made a quiet living attending to the civic orphans of the mechanical world: municipal tower clocks with seized striking trains, neglected barographs in coastal lifeboat stations, and, on this particular Tuesday, an Edwardian orrery stranded in the attic of a defunct maritime society.

Evelyn Shaw was waiting beneath the arched doorway of the Sallowpoint Athenaeum, holding a ring of iron keys and a wet canvas satchel. She worked for the district estate office, which meant her days were spent cataloguing things nobody wanted to pay to heat.

“You made good time from the junction,” she said, unlocking the heavy oak door. Inside, the vestibule held the flat, metallic chill of an unlived-in house. A staircase climbed sharply into gloom, its runners worn down to the pale warp threads. “I’m afraid the boiler gave up the ghost three winters back. If you need light, the circuit on the top floor still answers, though the skylight leaks a drop or two when the wind swings south.”

“Cold is fine,” Arthur said, wiping his boots twice on a coir mat that shed dry bristles. “Cold keeps the dust settled.”

They climbed two flights past framed charts of the Dogger Bank and yellowed photographs of bearded harbourmasters standing beside dreadnought anchors. On the top landing, Evelyn unlocked a pair of glazed double doors and stepped aside.

The gallery was long and narrow, lit by a grey wash of daylight pouring through dirty roof glass. Around the perimeter stood mahogany vitrines filled with tarnished sextants, whalebone scrimshaw, and pickled specimens in cloudy jars whose labels had curled into illegible scrolls. But the room existed for what stood in the center.

On a stout, octagonal plinth of dark walnut sat a grand floor-standing orrery, nearly four feet across. Its base was a deep mahogany drum banded in inlaid satinwood, supporting a broad, engraved brass horizon ring etched with the houses of the zodiac, the compass rose, and the calendar months in crisp Roman capitals. Above the plate, rising from a central sun-sphere the size of a billiard ball, slender brass arms cantilevered outward at staggered heights, each carrying a small painted or turned orb—Mercury close and cramped, Venus pale ivory, Earth tilted slightly on its axis with a pinhead moon, Mars dull copper, and outward through the gas giants to a distant, lonely Neptune, whose long steel arm drooped a quarter-inch from sheer age.

The whole miniature cosmos was veiled in a felt of grey dust. Nothing moved.

“The council’s liquidating the trust in the spring,” Evelyn said, resting her briefcase on a nearby case. “A developer wants the building for holiday flats. Most of the instruments are going to a dealer in Exeter, along with the charts. He’s offered a flat sum for the orrery as scrap-and-curio—brass weight plus novelty—unless it runs. If it runs, he’ll put it in the specialist auction in London.” She glanced at Arthur, her expression brisk and unsentimental. “I don’t need it restored to museum glory, Mr. Vance. I just need to know if the gears inside are stripped, or if it’s merely gummed up.”

Arthur walked slowly around the octagonal plinth, keeping his hands in his coat pockets. He leaned down until his eye was level with the horizon plate, squinting beneath the tangled forest of brass sleeves and concentric tubes that drove the planets around the central post.

“Who made it?” he asked.

“No maker’s plate,” Evelyn said. “The society’s minute books mention a local subscription in 1912. A Mr. Lindqvist had a marine instrument shop down by the old dry dock. Chronometers, binnacles, that sort of thing. They commissioned it for the centenary of the harbour wall.”

“Lindqvist,” Arthur murmured, testing the name. He reached out with one forefinger and touched the cold brass ball of Jupiter. It did not yield—not even the faint, springy backlash a healthy gear train offers when nudged. It felt rigid, as though the entire solar system had been cast in a single block of iron.

“There’s a winding key in the drawer beneath the plinth,” Evelyn said, checking her watch. “I have a valuation over at the old customs house at noon. Lock up if you step out for lunch—there’s a decent pasty shop down by the slipway, if it’s open on Tuesdays. I’ll check back Friday morning.”

When her footsteps had faded down the hollow stairs, Arthur took off his wool coat, draped it over a dusty display case, and put on a pair of spectacles with thick tortoiseshell rims. He drew a folded canvas drop-cloth from his bag and spread it across the wide worktable Evelyn had dragged beside the plinth. Then he unrolled his tools: graduated screwdrivers with boxwood handles, brass tweezers, slender lengths of orangewood for scraping verdigris without scarring softer metal, a bottle of penetrating oil, and a small tin of mutton tallow.

He found the brass winding key in the plinth drawer, wrapped in a piece of grey flannel. He did not insert it at once. A blind turn of a key in a seized clockwork machine is how teeth get sheared off pinions that haven’t been manufactured in a century. Instead, he knelt on the floorboards with a pocket torch and examined the underside of the mahogany drum, looking for access panels.

There were none. The entire mechanism was sealed within the drum, accessible only from above, beneath the engraved zodiac plate.

* * *

Taking a celestial machine apart is an exercise in humility, because every piece depends upon the symmetry of the piece beneath it. Arthur began at the outer edge of the sky. Using a small slotted driver, he loosened the tiny grub screws securing Neptune, Uranus, and Saturn, lifting each planet and its slender brass arm free and laying them in numbered order along the canvas sheet, as though he were dismantling a chandelier made of orbits.

By one o’clock, the heavens lay spread across the table in neat rows of dull gold and tarnished silver. Beneath the central sun-globe, the concentric brass sleeves—nested one inside another like the sections of a spyglass—rose from a wide circular brass cover plate. Arthur removed eight blued-steel screws around the rim, slipped the tips of two thin brass spatulas beneath the seam, and eased the heavy plate upward.

The smell that rose from inside the drum was not the sharp, rancid tang of old whale oil he had expected, nor the dusty dryness of neglect. It smelled faintly of camphor and cedar shavings.

Arthur angled his torch beam into the well of the mechanism.

The clockwork itself was magnificent—hand-cut brass wheels with slender, tapering spokes, steel arbors polished to a mirror sheen even after a hundred years, and a stout mainspring barrel paired with a brass fly-governor meant to keep the planets gliding at a smooth, unhurried pace rather than racing wildly whenever the spring was wound full. There was scarcely any rust. Whoever had sealed the drum had fitted the joints with oiled leather gaskets so tight that the damp sea air of Sallowpoint had never crept inside.

And yet the machine was locked solid.

Arthur leaned closer, adjusting the small magnifying loupe wedged into his right eye socket. Then he let out a slow breath through his nose.

Wedged firmly between the teeth of the great central crown wheel and the steel pinion driving the Earth’s sleeve was a thick, tapered sliver of *lignum vitae*—ironwood, dense as stone, commonly used by shipwrights for masthead sheaves and rudder bearings. Someone had not merely let the orrery run down. Someone had driven a wooden brake straight into its heart.

He took a pair of long-nosed pliers, gripped the protruding end of the wedge, and worked it gently side to side until it came free with a dry *tock*. Immediately, the tension in the mainspring gave a faint, metallic sigh, and the Earth’s sleeve shifted a fraction of an inch before the governor’s little brass paddles caught the air and held it steady.

Arthur stared at the wooden wedge in his palm. Its sides were scored where brass teeth had bitten into it under pressure. Someone had jammed it there while the spring was wound—which meant someone had stopped the sky mid-motion.

Before he touched the mainspring’s click to let down the power safely, he swept the beam of his torch around the shadowed perimeter of the mahogany drum. At the bottom, tucked neatly into the curved corner behind the mainspring barrel and secured by a loop of tarnished copper wire, lay a flat parcel wrapped in yellowed oilcloth.

Arthur unwound the wire with his fingers and lifted the parcel out. It was no bigger than a folded map. Inside the stiff, crackling oilcloth lay two things: a spare brass gear assembly mounted on a short steel bracket, and a narrow, cloth-bound surveyor’s notebook whose cover was mottled with damp rings.

He set the metal bracket on his canvas cloth under the lamp. It was a peculiar little mechanism—not a broken part awaiting replacement, because every tooth on its two small wheels was sharp and unworn. One wheel carried thirty-seven teeth; the other, fifty-three. Prime numbers, Arthur noted immediately, his brows drawing together. No sensible clockmaker pairs prime-numbered gears unless he wants an interval that refuses to divide evenly into days, months, or years. Mounted between them was an oblong, off-center steel cam, polished bright along one curved shoulder and dead flat on the other.

It belonged nowhere in a standard Copernican train. It had no planet attached to it, no pointer, no dial.

Arthur washed the oil and grime from his hands with a rag dipped in white spirit, pulled a rickety cane chair up to the table, and poured lukewarm tea from his thermos into its tin cap. The rain had started again, tapping a steady, impatient rhythm against the skylight overhead. Slowly, carefully, he opened the surveyor’s notebook.

* * *

The handwriting on the flyleaf was upright, deliberate, and slightly cramped, written with a fine steel nib that had caught now and then on the rough rag paper.

*C. Lindqvist. Workshop Ledger & Ratios — Harbour Centenary Commission. Commenced Oct. 1912.*

Arthur turned the pages slowly. The first twenty leaves were pure craft—lists of gear ratios calculated in neat columns of longhand multiplication, sketches of bevel teeth, complaints about a brass founder in Bristol who had sent a faulty casting for the zodiac ring, and notes on tempering the mainspring. Clara Lindqvist—for by page eight, a draft receipt signed *Clara Lindqvist, for Henrik Lindqvist & Sons* settled the initial—knew her trade thoroughly. Her calculations for Mercury’s eighty-eight-day sprint and Saturn’s thirty-year crawl were accurate to within a fraction of a percent, achieved with no more than standard lathes and a dividing engine.

Then, halfway through the book, three pages were torn out cleanly along the spine.

When the writing resumed on the following page, the date at the top read *November 19, 1913*. The nib was thicker now, the ink darker, pressed deep enough into the paper to raise ridges on the reverse side.

*No word from St. John’s,* the entry began. *The Admiralty cable this morning lists the Cormorant as twenty-two days overdue off Cape Farewell. Uncle Henrik says the pack ice came down early from Davis Strait, and the wireless set on a survey brigantine is good for nothing once the rigging freezes. Mother sits by the parlor grate with Martin’s brass dividers in her lap, measuring nothing.*

Arthur paused, looking up for a moment at the grey light washing down over the empty sextant cases. He thought of November on the North Atlantic—the short, iron-colored days, the heavy swell rolling down from Greenland before a man even knew the wind had shifted.

He turned the page.

*December 4, 1913. Uncle Henrik died Tuesday night, quietly, before the post came. The shop is mine now, though there is no trade in winter except repairing the trawler compasses. I cannot sleep past four. When the wind comes off the flats, I sit at the bench and finish the Centenary orrery, because the committee has already paid half the deposit and I cannot return what went into the Bristol castings.*

The entries grew sparser over the winter, separated by weeks, drifting back and forth between grief and mathematics.

*February 1914. Read Dr. Lowell’s paper again in the Society’s journal while waiting for the rosin bath to melt. He writes of the perturbations of Uranus and Neptune—that neither world follows the clean ellipse our equations demand, because something massive and unseen tugs at them from the dark beyond. He calls it Planet X. A ghost whose existence is proven solely by the way the visible things falter in their course.*

Arthur leaned forward, his elbows resting beside the disassembled orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

*March 1914. The committee wants a clean machine. Twelve months, three hundred and sixty-five days, a tidy brass clockwork world where nothing is lost and every ship arrives on its meridian. It seems a lie to build a sky that keeps smooth time when a boy who carried his sextant out of this very door is nowhere on the chart.*

*If an unseen body can make Neptune hesitate in its track, then what of a missing boat? I have cut two wheels in prime numbers—37 and 53—and a slow eccentric cam mounted to engage the Earth’s main sleeve. For three hundred and sixty-four turns of the horizon, the train runs true to Greenwich and the almanac. On the seventeenth revolution of the prime pair—falling near mid-November, by my count of the mainspring’s barrel—the cam lifts a brass shoe against the underside of the Earth’s collar. Not enough to break the teeth. Only enough to drag against the governor and make the world hesitate for four seconds—a slight, shuddering catch in the smooth turning of the heavens—before the cam drops clear and the planets resume their march.*

*I have set the bracket inside on trial bolts. It runs cleanly. No committee man will ever look beneath the zodiac plate, and if they hear the governor sigh once in a long while, they will blame a speck of dust in the oil.*

The final page contained no date, only a rough pencil diagram showing how the prime-numbered bracket bolted to two tapped holes inside the main baseplate, directly beneath the Earth’s concentric sleeve. Underneath, written in tiny, almost vertical letters, was a single line:

*Let it keep imperfect time. Perfection is for those who have lost nothing.*

Arthur sat back in the cane chair until its joints creaked. For several minutes, the only sound in the gallery was the rain running down the copper gutter outside the skylight.

He picked up the wooden wedge he had pried from the crown wheel and turned it over in his fingers. The story wrote itself easily enough across the hundred years between Clara’s bench and his own. Decades after the orrery had been wheeled into this upstairs room, someone—perhaps a caretaker, perhaps a neat-minded volunteer from the society—had stood watching the brass planets turn, had heard that sudden, inexplicable four-second drag in the middle of an autumn afternoon, and had assumed something inside was binding. Lacking the patience or the tools to dismantle the nested sleeves, they had lifted the cover plate just high enough to see the teeth, jammed a scrap of ironwood into the train to keep it from tearing itself apart, and closed the brass sky forever.

* * *

Arthur spent Wednesday and Thursday in a cocoon of quiet labor. He did not rush. When Evelyn’s municipal valuation didn’t pay enough to cover the hours he was spending, it did not matter; a man past fifty who repairs old clocks soon discovers that the unpaid hours are the only ones that belong entirely to him.

He stripped the entire movement down to its baseplate, washing each brass wheel in mineral spirits until the darkened, gummy film dissolved away, leaving the warm, pale gold of century-old alloy. He polished every steel arbor with boxwood slips and fine crocus powder, inspected the tiny ruby endstones set into the governor’s bridge under his loupe, and washed the coiled mainspring clean before dressing it lightly with fresh synthetic clock oil that would never turn to varnish as whale oil did.

When he came to Clara’s small steel bracket with its prime-numbered wheels, he hesitated for only a second before laying it into the cleaning bath alongside the rest.

The two tapped holes on the main baseplate were still there, plugged neatly with tiny brass blind screws so no grit could foul the threads. He backed the screws out, seated the bracket firmly into place, and checked the engagement of the off-center cam against the underside of the Earth’s brass sleeve. It was a brilliant piece of quiet engineering: the cam’s flat shoulder cleared the collar by the thickness of a sheet of foolscap paper for almost the entire cycle, but as the two prime wheels crawled out of phase and met at their lone common alignment, the curved lobe lifted smoothly, pressing a tiny strip of spring-tempered hornbeam against the collar—not a lock, just a gentle, mournful friction.

By Thursday dusk, the gallery was nearly dark, save for the small brass goose-neck lamp Arthur had plugged into the working outlet near the wainscot. The rain had thinned to a coastal mist that blurred the harbour lights down below.

He reassembled the concentric sleeves carefully, lowering the brass zodiac plate back over the drum and tightening its eight blued screws. One by one, he returned the planets to their posts: Mercury, Venus, Earth with its tiny ivory moon, copper Mars, banded Jupiter, ringed Saturn, pale Uranus, and finally long-armed Neptune, whose slight sag he corrected by delicately peening the brass collar at its root.

Then he took the winding key from the plinth drawer, slipped it through the small brass escutcheon on the side of the mahogany drum, and gave it six slow, measured turns.

Deep inside the wood, the mainspring tightened with a soft, rhythmic clicking of the ratchet. Arthur drew the key out and touched the tiny brass release lever tucked beneath the bezel of the zodiac ring.

For a heartbeat, nothing happened. Then, from inside the drum came a whisper like silk sliding over silk as the fly-governor spun up to speed.

Smoothly, almost imperceptibly, Mercury began to creep around the tarnished sun-globe. Venus followed at a steadier measure. Earth turned silently on its tilted pin, its tiny moon tracing quiet epicycles as it went. Arthur pulled his chair close, resting his chin on his folded hands on the edge of the table, and watched the clockwork sky move.

He had set the prime wheels just three teeth short of their alignment so he could witness it before morning. Ten minutes passed. Fifteen. Outside, the foghorn out on Sallowpoint breakwater let out a low, hollow moan that vibrated faintly through the floorboards.

Then the sound inside the mahogany drum altered.

The silky whir of the governor dropped half a tone, straining gently against an unseen weight. On its slender arm, the Earth seemed to tremble—not violently, just a faint, human hesitation, as though a breath were being caught mid-sentence. For four slow counts, the tiny globe dragged against the pull of its invisible companion. The other planets slowed in sympathy, bound together by the same brass spine. Then, with a faint, scarcely audible click, the cam cleared the collar. The governor sighed back up to pitch, and the solar system resumed its steady, unhurried glide across the months.

Arthur sat still for a long time after it passed, listening to the smooth, even pulse of the machine in the cold room.

* * *

Evelyn Shaw arrived at nine o’clock on Friday morning, carrying two cardboard cups of coffee from the corner café and a yellow clipboard tucked under her arm. She stopped just inside the glazed doors, her breath misting slightly in the chilly gallery, and stared toward the center of the room.

Beneath the grey skylight, the dust was gone. The mahogany drum gleamed softly from a coat of beeswax, the engraved Roman months caught the pale morning light, and the small brass planets moved in slow, stately silence around their sun.

“Good Lord,” she said softly, walking over and handing him one of the cups. “You worked miracles with it.”

“It didn’t need a miracle,” Arthur said, wrapping his stiff fingers around the warmth of the cardboard. “It wasn’t broken. Someone had just wedged a piece of ship’s timber into the crown wheel.”

Evelyn leaned down to peer closely at Mars as it crept past Leo, her expression softening for the first time since he had met her. “Why would anyone do that?”

Arthur glanced at the canvas tool roll, already buckled and ready beside his coat. Wrapped neatly inside his own pocket was the sliver of ironwood; Clara’s surveyor’s notebook lay back in its oilcloth inside the drum, tucked behind the mainspring barrel where he had found it, though he had added a small slip of acid-free paper inside the front cover recording the date of his cleaning and the oil used.

“People don’t always trust an irregular beat,” Arthur said simply. “If a machine doesn’t do what the textbook says it ought to do, they assume it’s faulty.”

Evelyn straightened up and clicked her pen, flipping open a fresh sheet on her clipboard. “Well, whatever the reason, it runs cleanly now. I’ll ring the auctioneer in Exeter this afternoon and tell him it’s a runner. Should add a fair bit to the trust’s final tally.” She paused, pen hovering over the page. “Before I write up the condition report—does it keep true time? If a collector asks, I need to know whether it gains or loses.”

Arthur looked back at the tiny painted Earth, moving steadily now along its brass ring toward December. In another fifty-three revolutions—nearly a year of quiet turning in someone’s drawing room or beneath a museum glass—that unseen, prime-numbered shadow would rise gently in the dark beneath the plate and ask the world to pause for four seconds. No collector in London would ever guess why, unless he happened to sit beside it on a damp November afternoon and listen closely enough.

“It keeps true time,” Arthur said, picking up his tool roll and lifting his coat from the vitrine. “True enough for anyone. And every now and then, it remembers something.”

Evelyn looked at him for a moment, uncertain whether he was making a watchmaker’s joke. Then she smiled slightly, wrote a brief note across the bottom of her sheet, and walked him back down the worn stairs to the street. Outside, the tide had turned, and the cold salt water was sliding back in across the mudflats, erasing the morning’s tracks one by one.

Arthur turned the pages slowly. The first twenty leaves were pure craft—lists of gear ratios calculated in neat columns of longhand multiplication, sketches of bevel teeth, complaints about a brass founder in Bristol who had sent a faulty casting for the zodiac ring, and notes on tempering the mainspring. Clara Lindqvist—for by page eight, a draft receipt signed *Clara Lindqvist, for Henrik Lindqvist & Sons* settled the initial—knew her trade thoroughly. Her calculations for Mercury’s eighty-eight-day sprint and Saturn’s thirty-year crawl were accurate to within a fraction of a percent, achieved with no more than standard lathes and a dividing engine.

Then, halfway through the book, three pages were torn out cleanly along the spine.

When the writing resumed on the following page, the date at the top read *November 19, 1913*. The nib was thicker now, the ink darker, pressed deep enough into the paper to raise ridges on the reverse side.

*No word from St. John’s,* the entry began. *The Admiralty cable this morning lists the Cormorant as twenty-two days overdue off Cape Farewell. Uncle Henrik says the pack ice came down early from Davis Strait, and the wireless set on a survey brigantine is good for nothing once the rigging freezes. Mother sits by the parlor grate with Martin’s brass dividers in her lap, measuring nothing.*

Arthur paused, looking up for a moment at the grey light washing down over the empty sextant cases. He thought of November on the North Atlantic—the short, iron-colored days, the heavy swell rolling down from Greenland before a man even knew the wind had shifted.

He turned the page.

*December 4, 1913. Uncle Henrik died Tuesday night, quietly, before the post came. The shop is mine now, though there is no trade in winter except repairing the trawler compasses. I cannot sleep past four. When the wind comes off the flats, I sit at the bench and finish the Centenary orrery, because the committee has already paid half the deposit and I cannot return what went into the Bristol castings.*

The entries grew sparser over the winter, separated by weeks, drifting back and forth between grief and mathematics.

*February 1914. Read Dr. Lowell’s paper again in the Society’s journal while waiting for the rosin bath to melt. He writes of the perturbations of Uranus and Neptune—that neither world follows the clean ellipse our equations demand, because something massive and unseen tugs at them from the dark beyond. He calls it Planet X. A ghost whose existence is proven solely by the way the visible things falter in their course.*

Arthur leaned forward, his elbows resting beside the disassembled orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

*March 1914. The committee wants a clean machine. Twelve months, three hundred and sixty-five days, a tidy brass clockwork world where nothing is lost and every ship arrives on its meridian. It seems a lie to build a sky that keeps smooth time when a boy who carried his sextant out of this very door is nowhere on the chart.*

*If an unseen body can make Neptune hesitate in its track, then what of a missing boat? I have cut two wheels in prime numbers—37 and 53—and a slow eccentric cam mounted to engage the Earth’s main sleeve. For three hundred and sixty-four turns of the horizon, the train runs true to Greenwich and the almanac. On the seventeenth revolution of the prime pair—falling near mid-November, by my count of the mainspring’s barrel—the cam lifts a brass shoe against the underside of the Earth’s collar. Not enough to break the teeth. Only enough to drag against the governor and make the world hesitate for four seconds—a slight, shuddering catch in the smooth turning of the heavens—before the cam drops clear and the planets resume their march.*

*I have set the bracket inside on trial bolts. It runs cleanly. No committee man will ever look beneath the zodiac plate, and if they hear the governor sigh once in a long while, they will blame a speck of dust in the oil.*

The final page contained no date, only a rough pencil diagram showing how the prime-numbered bracket bolted to two tapped holes inside the main baseplate, directly beneath the Earth’s concentric sleeve. Underneath, written in tiny, almost vertical letters, was a single line:

*Let it keep imperfect time. Perfection is for those who have lost nothing.*

Arthur sat back in the cane chair until its joints creaked. For several minutes, the only sound in the gallery was the rain running down the copper gutter outside the skylight.

He picked up the wooden wedge he had pried from the crown wheel and turned it over in his fingers. The story wrote itself easily enough across the hundred years between Clara’s bench and his own. Decades after the orrery had been wheeled into this upstairs room, someone—perhaps a caretaker, perhaps a neat-minded volunteer from the society—had stood watching the brass planets turn, had heard that sudden, inexplicable four-second drag in the middle of an autumn afternoon, and had assumed something inside was binding. Lacking the patience or the tools to dismantle the nested sleeves, they had lifted the cover plate just high enough to see the teeth, jammed a scrap of ironwood into the train to keep it from tearing itself apart, and closed the brass sky forever.

* * *

Arthur spent Wednesday and Thursday in a cocoon of quiet labor. He did not rush. When Evelyn’s municipal valuation didn’t pay enough to cover the hours he was spending, it did not matter; a man past fifty who repairs old clocks soon discovers that the unpaid hours are the only ones that belong entirely to him.

He stripped the entire movement down to its baseplate, washing each brass wheel in mineral spirits until the darkened, gummy film dissolved away, leaving the warm, pale gold of century-old alloy. He polished every steel arbor with boxwood slips and fine crocus powder, inspected the tiny ruby endstones set into the governor’s bridge under his loupe, and washed the coiled mainspring clean before dressing it lightly with fresh synthetic clock oil that would never turn to varnish as whale oil did.

When he came to Clara’s small steel bracket with its prime-numbered wheels, he hesitated for only a second before laying it into the cleaning bath alongside the rest.

The two tapped holes on the main baseplate were still there, plugged neatly with tiny brass blind screws so no grit could foul the threads. He backed the screws out, seated the bracket firmly into place, and checked the engagement of the off-center cam against the underside of the Earth’s brass sleeve. It was a brilliant piece of quiet engineering: the cam’s flat shoulder cleared the collar by the thickness of a sheet of foolscap paper for almost the entire cycle, but as the two prime wheels crawled out of phase and met at their lone common alignment, the curved lobe lifted smoothly, pressing a tiny strip of spring-tempered hornbeam against the collar—not a lock, just a gentle, mournful friction.

By Thursday dusk, the gallery was nearly dark, save for the small brass goose-neck lamp Arthur had plugged into the working outlet near the wainscot. The rain had thinned to a coastal mist that blurred the harbour lights down below.

He reassembled the concentric sleeves carefully, lowering the brass zodiac plate back over the drum and tightening its eight blued screws. One by one, he returned the planets to their posts: Mercury, Venus, Earth with its tiny ivory moon, copper Mars, banded Jupiter, ringed Saturn, pale Uranus, and finally long-armed Neptune, whose slight sag he corrected by delicately peening the brass collar at its root.

Then he took the winding key from the plinth drawer, slipped it through the small brass escutcheon on the side of the mahogany drum, and gave it six slow, measured turns.

Deep inside the wood, the mainspring tightened with a soft, rhythmic clicking of the ratchet. Arthur drew the key out and touched the tiny brass release lever tucked beneath the bezel of the zodiac ring.

For a heartbeat, nothing happened. Then, from inside the drum came a whisper like silk sliding over silk as the fly-governor spun up to speed.

Smoothly, almost imperceptibly, Mercury began to creep around the tarnished sun-globe. Venus followed at a steadier measure. Earth turned silently on its tilted pin, its tiny moon tracing quiet epicycles as it went. Arthur pulled his chair close, resting his chin on his folded hands on the edge of the table, and watched the clockwork sky move.

He had set the prime wheels just three teeth short of their alignment so he could witness it before morning. Ten minutes passed. Fifteen. Outside, the foghorn out on Sallowpoint breakwater let out a low, hollow moan that vibrated faintly through the floorboards.

Then the sound inside the mahogany drum altered.

The silky whir of the governor dropped half a tone, straining gently against an unseen weight. On its slender arm, the Earth seemed to tremble—not violently, just a faint, human hesitation, as though a breath were being caught mid-sentence. For four slow counts, the tiny globe dragged against the pull of its invisible companion. The other planets slowed in sympathy, bound together by the same brass spine. Then, with a faint, scarcely audible click, the cam cleared the collar. The governor sighed back up to pitch, and the solar system resumed its steady, unhurried glide across the months.

Arthur sat still for a long time after it passed, listening to the smooth, even pulse of the machine in the cold room.

* * *

Evelyn Shaw arrived at nine o’clock on Friday morning, carrying two cardboard cups of coffee from the corner café and a yellow clipboard tucked under her arm. She stopped just inside the glazed doors, her breath misting slightly in the chilly gallery, and stared toward the center of the room.

Beneath the grey skylight, the dust was gone. The mahogany drum gleamed softly from a coat of beeswax, the engraved Roman months caught the pale morning light, and the small brass planets moved in slow, stately silence around their sun.

“Good Lord,” she said softly, walking over and handing him one of the cups. “You worked miracles with it.”

“It didn’t need a miracle,” Arthur said, wrapping his stiff fingers around the warmth of the cardboard. “It wasn’t broken. Someone had just wedged a piece of ship’s timber into the crown wheel.”

Evelyn leaned down to peer closely at Mars as it crept past Leo, her expression softening for the first time since he had met her. “Why would anyone do that?”

Arthur glanced at the canvas tool roll, already buckled and ready beside his coat. Wrapped neatly inside his own pocket was the sliver of ironwood; Clara’s surveyor’s notebook lay back in its oilcloth inside the drum, tucked behind the mainspring barrel where he had found it, though he had added a small slip of acid-free paper inside the front cover recording the date of his cleaning and the oil used.

“People don’t always trust an irregular beat,” Arthur said simply. “If a machine doesn’t do what the textbook says it ought to do, they assume it’s faulty.”

Evelyn straightened up and clicked her pen, flipping open a fresh sheet on her clipboard. “Well, whatever the reason, it runs cleanly now. I’ll ring the auctioneer in Exeter this afternoon and tell him it’s a runner. Should add a fair bit to the trust’s final tally.” She paused, pen hovering over the page. “Before I write up the condition report—does it keep true time? If a collector asks, I need to know whether it gains or loses.”

Arthur looked back at the tiny painted Earth, moving steadily now along its brass ring toward December. In another fifty-three revolutions—nearly a year of quiet turning in someone’s drawing room or beneath a museum glass—that unseen, prime-numbered shadow would rise gently in the dark beneath the plate and ask the world to pause for four seconds. No collector in London would ever guess why, unless he happened to sit beside it on a damp November afternoon and listen closely enough.

“It keeps true time,” Arthur said, picking up his tool roll and lifting his coat from the vitrine. “True enough for anyone. And every now and then, it remembers something.”

Evelyn looked at him for a moment, uncertain whether he was making a watchmaker’s joke. Then she smiled slightly, wrote a brief note across the bottom of her sheet, and walked him back down the worn stairs to the street. Outside, the tide had turned, and the cold salt water was sliding back in across the mudflats, erasing the morning’s tracks one by one.
